steps.body: The standard algorithm counts the same groups, but fixes the batches by place value — one digit at a time, largest place first.
steps.narration: The standard algorithm counts the same groups, but fixes the batches by place value — one digit at a time, largest place first.

widget.prompt: Dividing 552 by 24, the first digit sits in the tens place — slide to what it is worth.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low — the first digit stands for whole tens of groups, not single ones.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — the tens digit here is 2, so it is worth twenty groups.
widget.successFeedback: 20 — the leading 2 sits in the tens place, standing for twenty groups of 24.

predict.prompt: In the standard algorithm, what fixes the batch sizes?
predict.reveal: Each digit's column decides its batch, which is exactly what makes the method compact.

cml.actionGoal: Count how many whole groups of the divisor fit, in whatever batches are convenient, for g5ld standard.
invariants: Division counts groups, and every method — estimating, partial quotients, the standard algorithm — counts the SAME groups in different batches, which is why g5ld standard always ends with quotient times divisor plus remainder rebuilding the dividend.
misconceptions: Placing a quotient digit a place out, treating an overshoot as final rather than adjusting the trial digit, or reporting a remainder that is as large as the divisor.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the remainder came out equal to the divisor, what would that tell you about the quotient?

widget.prompt: How does the standard algorithm differ from partial quotients?

options.label: It uses fixed place value batches
options.feedback: Correct — same counting of groups, but the batches are chosen for you, which is why it is compact and less forgiving.

options.label: It gives a different answer
options.feedback: Both count the same groups, so both reach the same quotient.

options.label: It does not use multiplication
options.feedback: Every step multiplies the divisor by a trial digit and subtracts the result.

options.label: It only works for one-digit divisors
options.feedback: It works for any divisor; two-digit ones simply make the trial digits harder to guess.

widget.prompt: In partial quotients, why may you take 20 groups of 24 before taking 3 more?

options.label: Groups may be removed in batches and totalled
options.feedback: Correct — the quotient counts groups, and counting them 20 at a time then 3 at a time gives the same 23.

options.label: Because 20 is always the right first step
options.feedback: The first batch is whatever is convenient; a different dividend would call for a different one.

options.label: Because the standard algorithm requires it
options.feedback: The standard algorithm fixes the batches by place value; partial quotients deliberately does not.

options.label: You may not — the batches must be equal
options.feedback: Unequal batches are the whole advantage of the method, provided they are totalled at the end.
